claims.claim: Virgil born 70 BC near Mantua, died 19 BC; wrote the Aeneid c. 29–19 BC and asked for it to be burned; Augustus had it published.
Octavian won at Actium in 31 BC and took the name Augustus in 27 BC; the doors of Janus were shut three times in his reign, twice before.

Jupiter's 'imperium sine fine dedi' (Aeneid I.279); Anchises' 'tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento' (VI.851–853); 'Italiam non sponte sequor' (IV.361); 'at pius Aeneas' (IV.393); 'hic amor, haec patria est' (IV.347); 'sum pius Aeneas' (I.378); 'timeo Danaos et dona ferentes' (II.49); 'sunt lacrimae rerum' (I.462).
claims.source: Virgil, Aeneid (Latin text, e.g. Perseus / Mynors OCT).

claims.claim: 'Parvulus Aeneas' (IV.328) is the only diminutive adjective in the Aeneid.
claims.source: R. G. Austin, Aeneid IV commentary (1955), on line 328.

claims.claim: Dido turns from Aeneas in silence in the underworld and returns to Sychaeus.
Punic Wars 264–146 BC; Cannae 216 BC; Carthage and Corinth destroyed 146 BC.
Purcell's Dido and Aeneas c. 1688 (libretto Nahum Tate); Dido's lament played at the Cenotaph on Remembrance Sunday; Berlioz, Les Troyens 1856–58.
claims.source: Grove Music Online; Royal British Legion order of service.

claims.claim: Augustine wept for Dido as a schoolboy.
Dante places Dido among the lustful.
Origen: God prepared the nations by uniting them under Rome so the apostles could travel.
Tacitus: Roman ways were called 'humanitas' by the ignorant when they were part of their slavery.
Battle of Mons Graupius AD 83 or 84; Agricola governor c. 77–84; Agricola written AD 98.
Plutarch: Caesar's Gallic wars killed a million and enslaved a million.
Citizenship extended to almost all free inhabitants in AD 212.
Paul's citizenship: Acts 22:25–28; appeal to Caesar Acts 25:11.
Polybius taken to Rome among 1,000 Achaean hostages in 167 BC; friend of Scipio Aemilianus; present at Carthage 146 BC; predicted Rome's decay.
claims.source: Polybius XXXI.23–25, XXXVIII.21–22, VI.57; Pausanias VII.10.11.

claims.claim: Cincinnatus dictator 458 BC, resigned after sixteen days.
Brutus executed his sons.
Washington resigned his commission in 1783; Society of the Cincinnati founded 1783; Cincinnati, Ohio, named 1790; The Federalist signed 'Publius'.
claims.source: Standard histories of the American founding.

claims.claim: Tiberius Gracchus killed 133 BC; Caesar crossed the Rubicon 49 BC, dictator for life early 44 BC, murdered 15 March 44 BC.
Cicero consul 63 BC; killed 7 December 43 BC near Formiae; head and hands displayed on the Rostra.
claims.source: Plutarch, Cicero 47–49; Appian, Civil Wars IV.19–20.

claims.claim: Pons Fabricius built 62 BC by L. Fabricius, curator viarum, still in use.
claims.source: Inscription on the bridge (CIL VI 1305); Cassius Dio 37.45.

claims.claim: Carneades' embassy to Rome 155 BC, arguing for and against justice; Cato hastened their departure.
claims.source: Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.14; Plutarch, Cato the Elder 22.

claims.claim: On the Commonwealth palimpsest found by Angelo Mai in the Vatican under Augustine on the Psalms, 1819, published 1822; the 'true law' passage survives in Lactantius, Divine Institutes VI.8.
Aquinas: an unjust law is 'not a law but a perversion of law'; first precept of natural law.
claims.source: Summa Theologiae I–II q.95 a.2; q.94 a.2.

claims.claim: Augustine: an unjust law seems to be no law.
claims.source: On Free Choice of the Will I.5.11.

claims.claim: Grotius: natural law would hold even if God did not exist (etiamsi daremus).
claims.source: De iure belli ac pacis (1625), Prolegomena 11.

claims.claim: Bentham: 'nonsense upon stilts'.
King quoted Augustine and Aquinas on unjust laws.
Spartacus revolt 73–71 BC; 6,000 crucified along the Appian Way.
400 slaves executed after the murder of Pedanius Secundus, AD 61.
Colosseum opened AD 80 with 100 days of games and 9,000 animals killed.
Josephus: 97,000 captured at Jerusalem.
Varro called slaves 'instrumentum vocale'.
Seneca, Letter 7, on the midday show: he came home 'more cruel and less human'. Taught in our own words.
Cicero calls crucifixion the most cruel and disgusting penalty.
Libido dominandi; 'remota iustitia quid sunt regna nisi magna latrocinia'; Rome never a true commonwealth.
claims.source: Augustine, City of God I preface, IV.4, XIX.21.

claims.claim: Constantine banned branding the face (316) and ended crucifixion.
claims.source: Theodosian Code 9.40.2; Aurelius Victor, De Caesaribus 41.4.

claims.claim: Telemachus killed trying to stop gladiators in Rome.
Gregory of Nyssa preached against slavery.
Institutes published 21 November 533, modelled on Gaius; Ulpian's definition of justice.
'Quod principi placuit legis habet vigorem'.
Digest rediscovered c. 1070; Irnerius at Bologna c. 1088; Gratian's Decretum c. 1140; Napoleonic Code 1804; BGB 1900.
claims.source: Peter Stein, Roman Law in European History (1999); Harold Berman, Law and Revolution (1983).

claims.claim: Justinian forbade forcing slaves into prostitution, eased marriage of freedmen.
Constantine read Eclogue IV as a prophecy of Christ.
claims.source: Constantine, Oration to the Assembly of the Saints 19–21.

claims.claim: Eclogue IV dedicated to Asinius Pollio, consul 40 BC; the 'Virgin' is Justice (Astraea).
Michelangelo painted five sibyls, including the Cumaean, on the Sistine ceiling.
Basilica of Maxentius begun c. 308, completed by Constantine after 312.
claims.source: Aurelius Victor 40.26; standard guides to the Forum.

claims.claim: Hagia Sophia completed 537; Constantinople founded 330 and fell 1453; last western emperor deposed 476.
Slave population of Italy perhaps 1–2 million at the end of the republic; roughly 10% across the empire.
claims.source: Walter Scheidel, JRS 95 (2005); Kyle Harper (2011). Figures uncertain, as the text says.
